summary.text: Gamma duplication and shift formulas rewrite the terms as an elementary quotient involving factorials and a product of consecutive odd factors, which is then decomposed into blocks of integers prime to \(p\). Pairings and permutations of the unit residues modulo \(p^r\) give \(v_p(\sum u^{-1})\ge 2r\) and \(v_p(\sum u^{-2})\ge r\); a third-order product expansion, together with parity-dependent block identities and a Morley-type product cancellation, shows the quotient of successive terms lies in \(1+p^{3r}\mathbb Z_p\), and integrality converts this to the desired integer congruence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(m)=\frac{\Gamma(9m+1)\Gamma(2m+1)\Gamma(3m/2+1)}
 {\Gamma(9m/2+1)\Gamma(4m+1)\Gamma(3m+1)\Gamma(m+1)}.
\]
We assume, as in the statement, that every \(a(m)\) is an integer. Fix a prime \(p\geq5\), and let \(|\cdot|_p\) be the normalized \(p\)-adic absolute value, so \(|p|_p=p^{-1}\). We prove the stronger intermediate assertion
\[
 \left|\frac{a(np^r)}{a(np^{r-1})}-1\right|_p\le p^{-3r}.                 \tag{1}
\]
The quotient in (1) will first be interpreted through a rational formula for \(a(m)\). At the end, the assumed integrality converts (1) into the required congruence.

Throughout the proof put \(P=p^t\), where \(t\geq1\), and introduce the following sets of \(p\)-adic units:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 U_t&=\{u:1\leq u\leq P,\ p\nmid u\},\\
 H_t&=\{d:1\leq d\leq P/2,\ p\nmid d\},\\
 W_t&=\{w:P/2<w\leq P/2+P,\ p\nmid w\},\\
 O_t&=\{y:1\leq y\leq2P,\ p\nmid y,\ 2\nmid y\}.
\end{aligned}                                                        \tag{2}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(P=2\lfloor P/2\rfloor+1\).

We shall repeatedly use the ultrametric inequality. In particular, if every summand in a finite sum has absolute value at most \(C\), then the whole sum has absolute value at most \(C\). We write
\[
 x\sim_k1\quad\text{if}\quad |x-1|_p\le p^{-k}.
\]
Products and positive integral powers of quantities \(\sim_k1\) are again \(\sim_k1\). If \(k\geq1\), such a quantity is a unit, its inverse is also \(\sim_k1\), and quotients of two such quantities are \(\sim_k1\).

We first establish the unit-sum estimates needed below:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{u\in U_t}u^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t},&
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{u\in U_t}u^{-1}\right|_p\le p^{-2t},\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{d\in H_t}d^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t},&
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{w\in W_t}w^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t},\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{w\in W_t}w^{-1}\right|_p\le p^{-2t},&
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{y\in O_t}y^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t},\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \left|\sum_{y\in O_t}y^{-1}\right|_p\le p^{-2t}.&
\end{array}                                                         \tag{3}
\]
Here and below all inverses are taken in \(\mathbb Q_p\).

We give the details. Multiplication by \(2\), reduced to the representative in \([1,P]\), permutes \(U_t\). Explicitly,
\[
 \sigma(u)=\begin{cases}2u,&2u\leq P,\\2u-P,&2u>P.\end{cases}
\]
Its inverse sends an even \(w\) to \(w/2\), and an odd \(w\) to \((w+P)/2\). For every \(u\in U_t\),
\[
 \sigma(u)^{-2}=\frac14u^{-2}+E_u,
 \qquad |E_u|_p\le p^{-t}.                                        \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the error is zero in the first case. In the second case direct subtraction gives
\[
 (2u-P)^{-2}-(2u)^{-2}
 =\frac{P(4u-P)}{4u^2(2u-P)^2},
\]
and all denominator factors are units. Summing (4), and denoting \(T=\sum_{U_t}u^{-2}\), yields
\[
 |T-\tfrac14T|_p\le p^{-t}.
\]
Since \(3\) and \(4\) are units for \(p\geq5\), this proves the first estimate in (3).

Next, the involution \(u\mapsto P-u\) permutes \(U_t\). Pairing a sum with its reindexed copy and using the exact identity
\[
 \frac1u+\frac1{P-u}
 =-\frac{P}{u^2}+\frac{P^2}{u^2(P-u)}                              \tag{5}
\]
shows
\[
 2\sum_{u\in U_t}u^{-1}
 =-P\sum_{u\in U_t}u^{-2}
   +P^2\sum_{u\in U_t}\frac1{u^2(P-u)}.
\]
The first term has absolute value at most \(p^{-2t}\) by the estimate just proved; the second does too because every denominator is a unit. Since \(2\) is a unit, this proves the second estimate.

The lower and upper halves of \(U_t\) correspond by \(d\mapsto P-d\). Consequently
\[
 \sum_{u\in U_t}u^{-2}
 =2\sum_{d\in H_t}d^{-2}+E,
 \qquad |E|_p\le p^{-t},                                          \tag{6}
\]
which follows by subtracting \((P-d)^{-2}\) from \(d^{-2}\); the difference has a factor \(P\) and a unit denominator. Thus the third estimate in (3) follows.

For completeness, the remaining window estimates follow from two elementary decompositions. For any function \(f\),
\[
 \sum_{w\in W_t}f(w)
 =\sum_{u\in U_t}f(u)+\sum_{d\in H_t}\bigl(f(d+P)-f(d)\bigr),      \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{y\in O_t}f(y)
 =\sum_{u\in U_t}f(u)
  +\sum_{\substack{u\in U_t\\2\mid u}}
       \bigl(f(u+P)-f(u)\bigr).                                   \tag{8}
\]
To see (7), an element in the lower half of \(U_t\) is shifted by \(P\), while an element in its upper half is left fixed. To see (8), shift precisely the even elements of \(U_t\) by the odd number \(P\); this produces exactly the odd units in \([1,2P]\).

For an arbitrary finite set \(V\) of units, if
\(\left|\sum_{v\in V}v^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t}\), then
\[
 \left|\sum_{v\in V}\bigl((v+P)^{-1}-v^{-1}\bigr)\right|_p
 \le p^{-2t}.                                                      \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, termwise expansion gives the exact formula
\[
 (v+P)^{-1}-v^{-1}=-Pv^{-2}+\frac{P^2}{v^2(v+P)}.
\]
Also, term by term,
\[
 |(v+P)^{-2}-v^{-2}|_p\le p^{-t},                                 \tag{10}
\]
because
\[
 (v+P)^{-2}-v^{-2}
 =-\frac{P(P+2v)}{v^2(v+P)^2}.
\]
The even units in \(U_t\) are exactly \(2d\), \(d\in H_t\), so their inverse-square sum is \(\frac14\sum_{H_t}d^{-2}\), of absolute value at most \(p^{-t}\). Applying (9) and (10) to (7) and (8), together with the already established estimates for \(U_t\) and \(H_t\), proves all of (3).

We next record the product estimate that is responsible for the exponent \(3t\). Suppose \(V\) is a finite set of units satisfying
\[
 \left|\sum_{v\in V}v^{-1}\right|_p\le p^{-2t},\qquad
 \left|\sum_{v\in V}v^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t},                  \tag{11}
\]
and suppose \(P\mid\Delta\). Then
\[
 \prod_{v\in V}\frac{v+\Delta}{v}\sim_{3t}1.                   \tag{12}
\]
To prove this, write \(z_v=\Delta/v\), so \(|z_v|_p\le p^{-t}\). The finite product has the second-order expansion
\[
 \prod_v(1+z_v)
 =1+\sum_vz_v+ rac{(\sum_vz_v)^2-\sum_vz_v^2}{2}+R,             \tag{13}
\]
where \(|R|_p\le p^{-3t}\). This remainder estimate follows directly by grouping all terms of degree at least three; equivalently, it follows by induction on the number of factors, using the ultrametric inequality. As \(2\) is a unit, division by \(2\) does not change norms. By (11),
\[
 \left|\sum_vz_v\right|_p
 =|\Delta|_p\left|\sum_vv^{-1}\right|_p\le p^{-3t},

a nd
\[
 \left|\sum_vz_v^2\right|_p
 =|\Delta|_p^2\left|\sum_vv^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-3t}.
\]
The square of the first sum is smaller still. Thus (13) proves (12). Products of any number of blocks (12) remain \(\sim_{3t}1\). By (3), this applies to \(V=U_t,W_t,O_t\), and also to every shift \(\Delta\) divisible by \(P\).

One additional, slightly subtler product is needed in the odd case. Set \(h=|H_t|\). We claim
\[
 2^{4h}\prod_{d\in H_t}\frac{d+P}{d}\sim_{3t}1.                  \tag{14}
\]
First we prove the exact elementary identity
\[
 2^h\prod_{d\in H_t}(P-2d)=\prod_{d\in H_t}(P-d).                \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, split \(U_t\) into its even and odd members. Its even members are \(2d\), \(d\in H_t\), so their product is
\(2^h\prod_{H_t}d\). Its odd members are \(P-2d\), \(d\in H_t\). On the other hand, splitting \(U_t\) into lower and upper halves gives
\[
 \prod_{u\in U_t}u=\left(\prod_{d\in H_t}d\right)
                    \left(\prod_{d\in H_t}(P-d)\right).
\]
Equating the two expressions and cancelling the positive product \(\prod d\) gives (15).

For \(d\in H_t\), define
\[
 w_d=\frac{P^2(4P-5d)}{d(P-2d)^2}.                                \tag{16}
\]
All denominator factors are units. Direct algebra, followed by (15), gives
\[
 2^{4h}\prod_{d\in H_t}\frac{d+P}{d}=\prod_{d\in H_t}(1+w_d).   \tag{17}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 1+w_d=\frac{4(P-d)^2(P+d)}{d(P-2d)^2},
\]
and multiplying this formula over \(d\), then replacing
\(\prod(P-d)\) by \(2^h\prod(P-2d)\), yields (17).

We have \(|w_d|_p\le p^{-2t}\), and a further exact calculation gives
\[
 \left|w_d+\frac54P^2d^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-3t}.                 \tag{18}
\]
For after multiplication by the unit \(4d^2(P-2d)^2\), the expression on the left becomes
\[
 P^3(5P-4d),
\]
which is divisible by \(P^3\). Summing (18), and using
\(\left|\sum_{H_t}d^{-2}\right|_p\le p^{-t}\), gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{d\in H_t}w_d\right|_p\le p^{-3t}.                 \tag{19}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 \left|\sum_{d\in H_t}w_d^2\right|_p\le p^{-4t}\le p^{-3t}.
\]
Applying the second-order product expansion (13), now with
\(|w_d|_p\le p^{-2t}\), proves that the right side of (17) is
\(\sim_{3t}1\), establishing (14).

We now turn to the factorial ratio. Define
\[
 D(M)=\prod_{j=0}^{M-1}(M+1+2j),                                  \tag{20}
\]
and
\[
 q(m)=\frac{2^{3m}(2m)!D(3m)}{(4m)!m!}.                            \tag{21}
\]
We first verify that \(q(m)=a(m)\). For positive \(x\) and an integer \(k\geq0\), repeated use of
\(\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)\) gives
\[
 \Gamma(x+k)=\Gamma(x)\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(x+j).                    \tag{22}
\]
Also the duplication formula is
\[
 \Gamma(x)\Gamma(x+\tfrac12)
 =2^{1-2x}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(2x).                                  \tag{23}
\]
Apply (23) at \(x=3m/2+1/2\) and \(x=9m/2+1/2\), and use (22) to write
\[
 \Gamma(9m/2+1/2)
 =\Gamma(3m/2+1/2)\prod_{j=0}^{3m-1}(3m/2+1/2+j).
\]
The product here equals
\[
 2^{-3m}\prod_{j=0}^{3m-1}(3m+1+2j)=2^{-3m}D(3m).
\]
Substituting these formulas into the defining gamma ratio cancels the two half-integral gamma values, \(\sqrt\pi\), \((9m)!\), and \((3m)!\), leaving exactly (21). This also holds for \(m=0\).

We next decompose the change from \(q(N)\) to \(q(Np)\). Put
\[
 F_p(M)=\prod_{\substack{1\leq j\leq M\\p\nmid j}}j,
\qquad
 D_p^*(M)=\prod_{\substack{0\leq j<Mp\\p\nmid Mp+1+2j}}
                    (Mp+1+2j).                                   \tag{24}
\]
Separating multiples of \(p\) gives the exact formulas
\[
 (mp)!=p^m m!F_p(mp),\qquad
 D(Mp)=p^M D(M)D_p^*(M).                                          \tag{25}
\]
For the second formula, the terms divisible by \(p\) occur at
\(j=(p-1)/2+kp\), \(0\leq k<M\), and are
\(p(M+1+2k)\).

Using (25) in (21), and cancelling the common power \(p^{5N}\), yields
\[
 \frac{q(Np)}{q(N)}=
 \frac{2^{3N(p-1)}F_p(2Np)D_p^*(3N)}
 {F_p(4Np)F_p(Np)}.                                                \tag{26}
\]
We shall prove that the right side is \(\sim_{3r}1\) when
\(N=np^{r-1}\).

The unit products in (26) break into blocks of length \(p^r\):
\[
 F_p(kp^r)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\prod_{u\in U_r}(u+ip^r).             \tag{27}
\]
Writing
\[
 U=\prod_{u\in U_r}u,
\]
we therefore have
\[
 F_p(kp^r)=U^k B_k,
\quad
 B_k=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\prod_{u\in U_r}\frac{u+ip^r}{u},         \tag{28}
\]
and (12) shows
\[
 B_k\sim_{3r}1.                                                    \tag{29}
\]
We need analogous decompositions of \(D_p^*(3N)\), and here parity matters.

First suppose \(n\) is even. Then \(3Np\) is even, and the numbers represented in \(D_p^*(3N)\) are precisely the odd \(p\)-units in the interval
\((3Np,3Np+6Np]\). Since \(Np=np^r\), this interval splits into
\(3n\) blocks of length \(2p^r\). Hence
\[
 D_p^*(3N)=\prod_{i=0}^{3n-1}\prod_{y\in O_r}
       \bigl(y+3Np+2ip^r\bigr).                                   \tag{30}
\]
If \(O=\prod_{y\in O_r}y\), then
\[
 D_p^*(3N)=O^{3n}C,
\quad
 C=\prod_{i=0}^{3n-1}\prod_{y\in O_r}
       \frac{y+3Np+2ip^r}{y}\sim_{3r}1,                           \tag{31}
\]
because every shift in (31) is divisible by \(p^r\), and (3), (12) apply to \(O_r\).

There is also the exact product identity
\[
 2^{|U_r|}\prod_{y\in O_r}y
 =\left(\prod_{u\in U_r}u\right)
   \prod_{u\in U_r}\frac{u+p^r}{u}.                              \tag{32}
\]
To prove it, split all \(p\)-units in \([1,2p^r]\) into the first and second blocks, and also into even and odd members. The even members are twice the members of \(U_r\). Cancelling the common product \(U\) gives (32). Denote the last product by \(Y\); by (12), \(Y\sim_{3r}1\).

The number of units in \(U_r\) is
\[
 |U_r|=p^r-p^{r-1}.                                                \tag{33}
\]
Since \(N=np^{r-1}\),
\[
 N(p-1)=n|U_r|.                                                     \tag{34}
\]
Thus
\(2^{3N(p-1)}=(2^{|U_r|})^{3n}\). Substitute (28), (31), and (32) into (26). All powers of \(U\) cancel:
\[
 \frac{q(Np)}{q(N)}
 =Y^{3n}\frac{B_{2n}C}{B_{4n}B_n}.                               \tag{35}
\]
Every factor on the right is \(\sim_{3r}1\), so (35) proves the desired estimate in the even case.

Now suppose \(n\) is odd. Then \(3N\), \(3Np\), and \(3n\) are odd. Put
\[
 A=\frac{3Np-1}{2}.
\]
Writing each term \(3Np+1+2j\) as \(2(A+1+j)\), and splitting the resulting interval into \(3n\) blocks of length \(p^r\), gives
\[
 D_p^*(3N)=2^{3Np-3N}
 \prod_{i=0}^{3n-1}\prod_{w\in W_r}
 \left(w+A-\frac{p^r}{2}+ip^r\right).                            \tag{36}
\]
Here integer division is intended in \(p^r/2\). The starting shift is divisible by \(p^r\), because
\[
 A-\frac{p^r}{2}=\frac{3n-1}{2}p^r.                              \tag{37}
\]
Formula (36) follows simply by translating the interval
\((A,A+3Np]\) to \((p^r/2,p^r/2+p^r]\) block by block and omitting multiples of \(p\). The factor \(2^{3Np-3N}\) appears because exactly \(3Np-3N\) of the \(3Np\) progression terms are not divisible by \(p\).

Let
\[
 W=\prod_{w\in W_r}w.
\]
By (3) and (12), (36) becomes
\[
 D_p^*(3N)=2^{3Np-3N}W^{3n}C',\qquad C'\sim_{3r}1.                \tag{38}
\]
Splitting \(W_r\) as in (7), but now for products, gives
\[
 W=U\prod_{d\in H_r}\frac{d+p^r}{d}.                            \tag{39}
\]
Also \(|U_r|=2|H_r|\), by the bijection between the lower and upper halves. From (34),
\[
 3N(p-1)+(3Np-3N)=4|H_r|\,(3n).                                  \tag{40}
\]
Indeed, each term on the left equals \(3N(p-1)\), and
\(N(p-1)=n|U_r|=2n|H_r|\).

Insert (28), (38), and (39) into (26), and use (40). Again all powers of \(U\) cancel, leaving
\[
 \frac{q(Np)}{q(N)}
 =\left(2^{4|H_r|}\prod_{d\in H_r}\frac{d+p^r}{d}\right)^{3n}
   \frac{B_{2n}C'}{B_{4n}B_n}.                                   \tag{41}
\]
The parenthesized factor is \(\sim_{3r}1\) by (14), and all the block factors are \(\sim_{3r}1\) by (12). Thus (41) proves
\[
 \left|\frac{q(Np)}{q(N)}-1\right|_p\le p^{-3r}                 \tag{42}
\]
in the odd case as well. Together with the even case, (42) holds for every positive \(n\), with \(N=np^{r-1}\).

It remains to convert the rational quotient estimate into an integer congruence. Let
\[
 A=a(Np),\qquad B=a(N).
\]
By hypothesis these are integers, and by the gamma calculation they equal \(q(Np)\) and \(q(N)\), respectively. The rational number \(q(N)\) is nonzero, since its numerator and denominator in (21) are positive. Moreover \(|B|_p\le1\), because \(B\) is an integer. Therefore (42) gives
\[
 |A-B|_p
 =\left|B\left(\frac{A}{B}-1\right)\right|_p
 \le p^{-3r}.                                                     \tag{43}
\]
For an integer \(z\), the inequality \(|z|_p\le p^{-k}\) is equivalent to \(p^k\mid z\). Applying this to (43) yields
\[
 p^{3r}\mid a(np^r)-a(np^{r-1}).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 \boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r}}},
\]
for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\), as required.
